Write the first page of an onboarding document for a new backend engineer joining a payments team. Around 200 words.

# Welcome to Payments

## What this team owns

We move money. Every service in this repo either authorizes a charge, settles a batch, or reconciles what the processor tells us against what our ledger says. If those three disagree, someone's money is in the wrong place, and that is the failure mode we design around.

Your first two weeks are mostly reading. Start with `ledger-core`, because everything else assumes you know how a double-entry posting works here. A charge writes two rows, never one. There is no update path on a posted entry; corrections are new entries that offset the old ones. This trips up almost everyone who arrives from CRUD-shaped systems.

## Before you write code

Get your access sorted on day one, since approvals take about three days:

- Sandbox processor credentials, from your onboarding ticket
- Read access to the production ledger replica (read only, and it stays that way)
- PagerDuty, so you can shadow the on-call rotation in week two

## The rule that matters most

Idempotency keys are required on every write path that touches an external processor. A retried request without one can charge a customer twice, and we have done it before. The interface in `payments/idempotency.go` shows the pattern; use it rather than rolling your own key derivation.

Ask questions in #payments-eng. Nobody here expects you to be productive in week one.

## Who to ask for what

Ask a person before you ask a search box. Everyone here would rather answer a question twice than debug a duplicate charge.

- Priya handles ledger and posting semantics. She wrote most of `ledger-core` and can tell you why a rule exists, not only what it says.
- Marcus handles processor integrations and sandbox credentials. He also unblocks you when the sandbox returns a decline you cannot explain.
- Dana handles settlement and reconciliation jobs. Batch timing is fussier than the code suggests, and she knows which nightly failures are expected noise.
- Sam handles deploys, on-call, and alert routing. Use #payments-oncall if it is urgent and Sam is asleep.
- Ravi, your manager, handles scope and priorities, including whether a task is worth doing at all. Your weekly 1:1 starts Thursday, but you don't have to hold questions for it.

For compliance questions (refund windows, data retention, what we are allowed to log about a card), post in #payments-eng and tag the risk team instead of guessing. Those answers are legal as often as technical, and a wrong guess costs us an audit finding.

There is one norm worth knowing early. If you are stuck for more than about forty minutes on something that isn't yours to own yet, that is the signal to ask. Nobody tracks who asked what. We do track charges that went out twice.
